## R Markdown

```{r}
#Part A

#Question 1A
shoe_size <- c(6.5, 9.0, 8.5, 8.5, 10.5, 7.0, 9.5, 9.0, 13.0, 7.5,
               10.5, 8.5, 12.0, 10.5, 13.0, 11.5, 8.5, 5.0, 10.0, 6.5,
               7.5, 8.5, 10.5, 8.5, 10.5, 11.0, 9.0, 13.0)

height <- c(66.0, 68.0, 64.5, 65.0, 70.0, 64.0, 70.0, 71.0, 72.0, 64.0,
            74.5, 67.0, 71.0, 71.0, 77.0, 72.0, 59.0, 62.0, 72.0, 66.0,
            64.0, 67.0, 73.0, 69.0, 72.0, 70.0, 69.0, 70.0)

gender <- c("F", "F", "F", "F", "M", "F", "F", "M", "M", "F",
            "M", "F", "M", "M", "M", "M", "F", "F", "M", "F",
            "F", "M", "M", "F", "M", "M", "M", "M")

shoesize <- data.frame(shoe_size, height, gender)

write.csv(shoesize, "shoesize.csv", row.names = FALSE)

shoesize

#Question 1B
shoesize <- read.csv("shoesize.csv")

tail(shoesize, 5)

#Question 1C
str(shoesize)

#Question 1D
dim(shoesize)
nrow(shoesize)
ncol(shoesize)

#Question 1E
summary(shoesize)
#str() tells you what the data looks like, while summary() tells you what the data contains statistically.

#Question 1F
males   <- shoesize[shoesize$gender == "M", ]
females <- shoesize[shoesize$gender == "F", ]

males
females

#Question 1G
mean(shoesize$shoe_size)
mean(shoesize$height)

#Question 1H
cor(shoesize$shoe_size, shoesize$height)
#Yes, there is a moderate to strong positive relationship. A correlation of 0.66 indicates that as shoe size increases, height tends to increase as well.

#Question 2
shoesize$gender <- factor(shoesize$gender)

levels(shoesize$gender)
shoesize$gender

#Question 3
#This makes an R Markdown document more reliable because it always looks for files in the same folder where the .Rmd file is saved. This means that when someone else opens and runs the document, the imported files are easier to find, even if their working directory is different. It helps make the results more consistent and reproducible.

#Question 4
str(shoesize)
#The Gender column is usually assigned as a character or factor, which is expected because it contains text values. If a column like ShoeSize is accidentally imported as character, R might not be able to perform mathematical operations or calculations properly. This could lead to errors or incorrect results in the analysis.

#Question 5
#It is good to check both head(shoes) and tail(shoes) because head() only shows the first few rows, while tail() shows the last few rows. Checking both helps us see if the data was imported completely and correctly. For example, head() alone might not catch missing values, incorrect entries, or formatting problems at the end of the file.

#Question 6A
cor(shoesize$shoe_size, shoesize$height)

#Question 6B
shoesize[shoesize$shoe_size >= 11, ]

#Question 7
# Mean height by gender
mean(males$height)
mean(females$height)

# Mean shoe size by gender
mean(males$shoe_size)
mean(females$shoe_size)

#The comparison helps show the differences in average height and shoe size between females and males. Generally, males may have higher average height and shoe size than females. This suggests that gender could be an important factor when studying the relationship between height and shoe size. We should compare the relationship within each gender separately because gender differences might affect the overall results.
```
